To anoint someone means to deliberately apply oil — or sometimes another liquid — to a person's body, usually as a meaningful, ceremonial act. But the word almost never stops at just the physical action. Anointing is almost always done for a reason: to bless, consecrate, honor, or mark someone as specially chosen.

This is the key insight: if you pour cooking oil into a frying pan, you don't anoint it. But if a priest pours sacred oil on a person's head during a religious ceremony, that is anointing. The difference is purpose and significance. Anointing is never casual — it always carries weight.

1. The Literal, Ceremonial Meaning

This is the original and oldest use of the word. Anointing with oil is one of humanity's most ancient rituals, practiced across many religions and cultures. In this sense, to anoint someone means to apply oil to them as a sacred act — to bless them, purify them, or officially mark them as set apart for a holy or important purpose.

People have been anointed for many reasons throughout history:

  • To install them as a king, priest, or leader (the oil symbolizes divine blessing and authority)
  • To consecrate them — meaning to make them sacred or dedicated to God
  • To heal them — in many religious traditions, anointing the sick is an act of prayer and care
  • To prepare a body for burial (this appears in ancient texts including the Bible)

Examples in sentences:

  • "The high priest anointed the new king with oil, marking the beginning of his reign."
  • "During the ceremony, the bishop anointed the young man's hands as he became a priest."
  • "The women came to anoint Jesus's body after the crucifixion."

One fact that shows you how central this concept is to religion: the word Messiah in Hebrew and Christ in Greek both literally mean "the anointed one" — a person who has been chosen and set apart by God. That tells you everything about the spiritual weight this word carries.

2. The Figurative Meaning — To Officially Choose or Declare Someone

Over time, "anoint" moved beyond religion into everyday language. Today, it is very commonly used figuratively to mean: to officially select, declare, or endorse someone as especially important — typically as a future leader, successor, or top choice — usually because someone powerful or influential is doing the choosing.

In this figurative use, no oil is involved at all. It's purely about the idea of elevation and selection.

Examples in sentences:

  • "The retiring CEO anointed her deputy as the company's next leader."
  • "The senior politicians anointed him as their preferred candidate long before the election."
  • "By giving him the most prestigious project, the director essentially anointed him as the team's rising star."

Notice the common thread: in every example, someone with authority is choosing someone else and lifting them up. This is crucial — anointing is not something you do to yourself. It comes from above. A king doesn't anoint himself; a priest, a prophet, or a powerful figure does it. Similarly, in the figurative sense, you don't anoint yourself as a leader — others do it for you.

3. A General, Non-Religious Literal Use

Occasionally, "anoint" is used simply to mean to apply oil or liquid to someone's body, with no religious meaning at all.

  • "She anointed her skin with warm coconut oil."
  • "The healer anointed the wound with herbal oil."

This use is less common in everyday conversation — most people would just say "rubbed" or "applied." Using "anoint" here sounds elevated, old-fashioned, or literary. But you will encounter it, especially in older texts.
The Feeling the Word Always Carries

Across all its uses, "anoint" consistently carries one feeling: being set apart from the ordinary. An anointed person is not just assigned a role — they are elevated, chosen, blessed. There is almost always a sense of ceremony, destiny, or special status attached to the word. This is what separates it from plainer words like "choose," "appoint," or "select."
How to Use It in a Sentence

Anoint almost always follows this structure:

[Someone] anoints [someone] [with something] [as something]

  • "The priest anointed the child with holy oil." (with = the substance used)
  • "The board anointed her as the next chairperson." (as = the role she is elevated to)
  • "He was anointed the heir by the outgoing leader."

Anointed (adjective or past tense verb): Describes someone who has been anointed.

  • "She is the anointed successor."
  • "The king was anointed at dawn."

Anointing (noun or present participle): The act of applying oil or the broader act of choosing.

  • "The anointing of the sick is a holy sacrament in Catholicism."
  • "His anointing as the next leader surprised many."

Anointment (noun): The result or act of anointing.

  • "Her anointment as champion was celebrated by her supporters."

The Anointed One (phrase): A title for someone divinely chosen — most famously used to refer to the Messiah or Christ.

Self-anointed (adjective): This is a critically used phrase. It describes someone who declares themselves to be special, important, or an authority — without being genuinely chosen or recognized by others. It is almost always used to mock or dismiss someone.

  • "He is a self-anointed expert with no real credentials."
  • "She is the self-anointed voice of the people."
Anoint vs. Appoint — Don't Confuse Them

These two words sound similar and both involve placing someone in a role, but they feel very different.

Appoint is practical and neutral. It simply means to officially give someone a job or role.

  • "She was appointed as the new head of the department." — No ceremony, no grand significance. Just an assignment.

Anoint is grander, more ceremonial, and implies a sense of being "the chosen one."

  • "She was anointed as the future of the company." — This suggests she's been singled out as exceptional, blessed by those in power, destined for greatness.

If your manager emails you saying you got a promotion, that's an appointment.
If your manager publicly declares you to be the future star of the organization and everyone starts treating you differently, that's closer to anointment.

To anoint someone means to apply oil to them — usually as part of a religious ceremony — in order to bless them, consecrate them, or officially mark them as chosen for an important role. By extension, it means to officially select or endorse someone as special or as a future leader, without any literal oil involved. The word always carries a sense of elevation, ceremony, and being set apart from the ordinary. It implies that someone with authority has deliberately lifted another person up and marked them as significant. The opposite of this feeling would be something bland and bureaucratic — anointing is always meaningful, always carries weight, and always suggests that the person receiving it is no longer ordinary.
